lead: An electronic ignition system replaces the contact breaker with a sensor and a transistor. The transistor switches the coil's primary current, and an ignition module or the engine ECU decides when to start that current and when to stop it. Programmed ignition goes further: it stores the spark advance in a map indexed by engine speed and load (manifold pressure or air flow), then corrects the mapped value for coolant temperature, knock and starting. You meet it on almost every petrol car and motorcycle sold today.
prereq: You need: dwell, the coil current curve and advance from ignition fundamentals.

sections.h3: From points to a transistor switch

blocks.text: The contact breaker has three problems as engines get faster. The points burn, because they break a few amperes many times a second. The dwell angle drifts as the rubbing block wears, so the coil current changes. And at high speed the fixed dwell angle lasts too short a time to build full current, and the points may bounce.

Electronic ignition removes the rubbing block. An inductive (magnetic reluctance) or Hall-effect pick-up in the distributor or at the crankshaft sends a pulse each time a trigger-wheel tooth passes. The pulse tells the module the crank angle. The module drives a power transistor, often called the igniter, in series with the coil primary. The pick-up only reports position; a small signal from it controls the large coil current.

Early modules kept the points' behaviour. In a constant-dwell system the dwell angle is fixed, as with points, so the dwell time shrinks as speed rises. A constant-energy system uses a low-inductance, low-resistance coil that reaches its current quickly. It measures the coil current and switches the transistor on just early enough to reach a set current, about 7–8 A, before each spark; a current-limiting circuit then holds that current until the break. So the dwell time stays nearly constant and the dwell angle grows with speed. It also lengthens the dwell when the battery voltage is low. At very high speed the dwell angle reaches its limit and the energy finally falls.

blocks.where: t<sub>d</sub> is the dwell time in seconds, D the dwell as a fraction of the spark interval and T<sub>s</sub> = 120 ÷ (N × z) the spark interval in seconds, with N the speed in rev/min and z the number of cylinders of a four-stroke engine.

blocks.text: Programmed ignition, also called electronic spark advance or digital ignition, stores the spark timing in a table in the ECU memory. One axis is engine speed, the other is load (manifold pressure or air flow per stroke). Each cell holds an advance in degrees before TDC (BTDC); a typical map has 16 speeds × 16 loads, and between cells the ECU interpolates. Drawn in three dimensions the table looks like a rough landscape, the ignition map. Unlike centrifugal weights and a vacuum diaphragm, the map can take any shape the calibrator finds best on the test bed.

The ECU then corrects the mapped value. Coolant temperature: extra advance on a cold engine. Knock: the ECU retards the spark in small steps when the knock sensor reports detonation, then advances it back slowly. Starting: a fixed safe advance during cranking. It also sets the dwell from battery voltage and speed, using a second, smaller map.

The chain has these blocks: a crank sensor (speed and crank angle) with a reference mark for TDC; a manifold pressure or air-flow sensor (load); coolant temperature and knock sensors; the ECU with its maps; the igniter; the coil; and, on older systems, a distributor sending the high voltage to the plugs in the firing order. Later systems drop the distributor (see distributorless and direct ignition).

The ECU sends a dwell pulse to the igniter. The rising edge starts the primary current; the falling edge stops it and fires the spark. The time between the two edges is the dwell time, and the angle between the falling edge and TDC is the spark advance. Because both are computed from crank-sensor teeth, the timing stays correct for the life of the engine and needs no adjustment.

Four control methods appear in order of increasing freedom. Mechanical control uses centrifugal and vacuum advance and cannot correct for temperature. Electronic control replaces the points with a transistor but may keep a mechanical advance curve. Mapped control reads a table, so the advance can follow any shape. Closed-loop knock control adds feedback: it retards when knock appears and advances back until knock just reappears, so the engine runs close to its knock limit without damage.

A service technician sees the result as a scan-tool data stream: rpm, manifold pressure, coolant temperature, calculated advance, knock retard and dwell. A failed crank sensor usually stops the spark altogether; a failed knock sensor usually makes the ECU fall back to a safe, retarded map.

examples.question: A four-cylinder four-stroke petrol engine runs at 5000 rpm on a constant-dwell system with dwell of 60% of the spark interval. The knock sensor requests 4° of retard. Find the spark rate, the spark interval, the dwell time and the time taken by 4° of crank rotation.
steps: One revolution takes 60/5000 s = 12 ms for 360°, so 4° takes 4 × 12/360 = 0.133 ms.
examples.answer: 166.7 sparks/s; spark interval 6 ms; dwell time 3.6 ms; the 4° retard moves the spark 0.133 ms later.

examples.question: A constant-energy system's coil needs 3.0 ms of current to reach its limited current of 7.5 A. For a four-cylinder four-stroke engine find the dwell as a fraction of the spark interval and as a crank angle at 1000 rpm and at 6000 rpm.
steps: Spark interval at 1000 rpm: T<sub>s</sub> = 120 ÷ (1000 × 4) = 0.030 s = 30 ms.
Fraction = 3.0 ÷ 30 = 0.10; the angle between sparks is 720°/4 = 180°, so the dwell angle = 0.10 × 180° = 18° of crank.
Spark interval at 6000 rpm: T<sub>s</sub> = 120 ÷ (6000 × 4) = 0.005 s = 5 ms.
Check: 18° at 1000 rpm lasts 18/360 × 60 ms = 3.0 ms, and 108° at 6000 rpm lasts 108/360 × 10 ms = 3.0 ms.
examples.answer: At 1000 rpm the dwell is 10% of the interval, 18° of crank; at 6000 rpm it is 60%, 108° of crank. The dwell time stays 3.0 ms, so every spark gets the same 7.5 A.

traps: Swapping the two systems. Constant dwell keeps the dwell angle (as points did), so dwell time falls with speed; constant energy keeps the coil current, so the dwell angle rises with speed.
Mixing spark advance with dwell. Advance is when the spark occurs relative to TDC; dwell is the charging period before it.
Forgetting the z/2 factor for a four-stroke engine. N/60 alone gives one spark per revolution.
Reading the map's load axis as accelerator pedal position. Advance maps use manifold pressure or air flow.
Thinking knock retard is permanent. The ECU retards only while knock is present, then creeps back toward the mapped value.

quiz.q: What is dwell in an electronic ignition system?
quiz.a: The time for which the igniter lets primary current flow in the coil before the spark, in milliseconds or as a fraction of the spark interval.

quiz.q: Why did electronic ignition replace the contact breaker?
quiz.a: The points burn because they break several amperes, their dwell drifts as the rubbing block wears, and at high speed the fixed dwell lasts too short a time. A transistor and a position sensor remove all three problems.

quiz.q: A six-cylinder four-stroke engine runs at 3000 rpm with dwell of 50% of the spark interval. Find the spark interval and dwell time.
Why does a constant-energy system lose spark energy only at very high speed, while a constant-dwell system loses it steadily?
quiz.a: The constant-energy system keeps the dwell time (about 3 ms here) by raising the dwell angle as speed rises, so the coil reaches its set current until the needed angle runs into its limit. The constant-dwell system keeps the angle, so its dwell time and coil current fall with every rise in speed.

quiz.q: Name two pick-ups used in electronic ignition in place of the contact breaker.
quiz.a: The inductive (magnetic reluctance) pick-up and the Hall-effect pick-up.

quiz.q: Which corrections does programmed ignition add to the mapped advance?
quiz.a: Coolant temperature, knock retard and a fixed cranking advance; many systems also correct for intake air temperature. Speed and load are the map's axes, not corrections.

quiz.q: A four-cylinder four-stroke engine runs at 4000 rpm. How much time does 5° of crank rotation take?
quiz.a: One revolution takes 60/4000 s = 15 ms, so 5° takes 5 × 15/360 = 0.208 ms.

quiz.q: Compare mapped ignition control with closed-loop knock control.
quiz.a: Mapped control reads the stored advance for the present speed and load and does not check the result: it is open loop. Knock control adds a sensor and feedback: it retards when detonation is detected and advances back slowly, so the engine runs at the knock limit for the fuel actually in the tank.

beyond: Modern ECUs control knock cylinder by cylinder and some read the ionisation current through the plug to see combustion directly. Model-based calibration fills the map from engine models instead of only bench sweeps. Search terms: ignition map calibration, individual cylinder knock control, ion current sensing.
